questions.prompt: What is Salesforce DX?
options: A dedicated Salesforce edition sold only to ISV partners
A reporting dashboard for tracking deployment history
Salesforce's source-driven development methodology and toolchain, built around the Salesforce CLI, scratch orgs, and packaging
A deprecated name for the Developer Console
questions.explain: Salesforce DX is a development methodology and toolchain — the Salesforce CLI, scratch orgs, source format, and packaging — built around source-driven development, where local version-controlled files are the source of truth.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes a licensing arrangement, not a development methodology — Dev Hub (which some orgs enable) is unrelated to ISV-only editions. Salesforce DX is available on production, Developer Edition, and trial orgs alike, not a separate edition.

questions.prompt: A team wants to enable Dev Hub on an org so they can create scratch orgs. Which org type can they NOT use?
options: A production org
A Developer Edition org
A trial org
A sandbox
questions.explain: Sandboxes cannot be enabled as a Dev Hub — only production, Developer Edition, and trial orgs qualify, and once enabled on any of those, it cannot be disabled.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: if you don't specify --duration-days when creating a scratch org, it defaults to ________ days before expiring.
questions.explain: The --duration-days flag accepts a value from 1 to 30 days, and defaults to 7 days when not specified.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about scratch orgs.
options: They are source-tracked by default
They can be created from a definition file, an edition flag, a snapshot, or an org shape
Once expired, an already-expired scratch org's contents can be recovered by extending its duration
They are meant to be disposable rather than long-lived like a sandbox
A scratch org's duration can be set anywhere from 1 to 30 days
questions.explain: Scratch orgs are source-tracked by default, can be created four ways (definition file, edition, snapshot, or org shape), are intentionally disposable, and can be set to live 1-30 days. There is no way to extend or recover an already-expired scratch org — that claim is false.

questions.prompt: A scratch org definition file needs to match the features, settings, and licenses of an existing production org exactly. Which property should it use instead of `edition`?
options: adminEmail
sourceOrg, set to the production org's 15-character org ID
hasSampleData
language
questions.explain: Matching an existing org's shape uses the sourceOrg property, set to that org's 15-character org ID, in place of specifying edition directly.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.
right: The flatter, zip-oriented layout used by raw Metadata API deploy/retrieve calls
A model where local, version-controlled files are the source of truth, not the org
A regular org with a setting enabled that lets it create scratch orgs and packages
A disposable, source-tracked org created on demand for development and testing
questions.explain: Dev Hub is a regular org with scratch-org/packaging capability enabled; a scratch org is the disposable, source-tracked org it creates; source-driven development makes local files the source of truth; Metadata API format is the flatter, zip-oriented layout used for raw API calls, distinct from source format.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order to go from nothing to a running scratch org.
items: Enable Dev Hub in Setup on a production, Developer Edition, or trial org
Authenticate the CLI to that org with sf org login web --set-default-dev-hub
Write a scratch org definition file under config/
questions.explain: Dev Hub must be enabled first, then the CLI authenticated to it, then a definition file written describing the desired scratch org shape, and finally the scratch org actually created referencing both the Dev Hub and the definition file.

questions.prompt: What is a key downside of enabling Dev Hub on a trial or Developer Edition org rather than a stable production org, for real team use?
options: Trial orgs cannot run Apex code
If the trial or Developer Edition org expires, every package and scratch org allocation tied to it is lost
Trial orgs are not allowed to authenticate with the CLI at all
Developer Edition orgs cannot have a namespace
questions.explain: Because Dev Hub enablement is tied to that specific org, losing access to a trial or Developer Edition org (through expiration) means losing access to everything built on top of it as a Dev Hub.

questions.prompt: What is sfdx-project.json?
options: A log of every scratch org ever created
The root configuration file of a Salesforce DX project, declaring its package directories, namespace, and API version
A backup file generated after every deploy
The file that stores a user's login password for the CLI
questions.explain: sfdx-project.json is the root configuration file every Salesforce DX project requires, defining packageDirectories, namespace, sourceApiVersion, and related project-level settings.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes something closer to `sf org list` output, not a project configuration file — sfdx-project.json describes the project's structure and settings, not a history of created orgs.

questions.prompt: A project has two entries in packageDirectories: force-app and utils-package. Neither is marked "default": true. What's the issue?
options: This is fine — the CLI never needs a default when there's more than one package directory
This violates the requirement that exactly one entry must be marked default when there are multiple package directories
The project will refuse to generate any new metadata at all
Only the first alphabetically-named directory is ever used as default
questions.explain: With a single package directory, the default is assumed automatically; with more than one, exactly one entry must be explicitly marked default, since default-dependent operations like pulling changes need an unambiguous target.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in a package.xml manifest, the metadata type name used to retrieve or deploy Apex classes is ________.
questions.explain: ApexClass is the metadata type name used in a package.xml <types><name> element to reference Apex class components.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Metadata API.
options: It moves an org's configuration — object/field definitions, Apex, Flows, Permission Sets — not record data
Every metadata type has identical, full support for every Metadata API operation
package.xml names specific components or entire types (via wildcards) to retrieve or deploy
sf project deploy start and sf project retrieve start are, under the hood, Metadata API deploy/retrieve calls
The Metadata API is used primarily to move Account and Contact record data between orgs
questions.explain: The Metadata API moves configuration, not data (so the last option is false); package.xml names types/components with wildcards or specific members; the sf project deploy/retrieve commands are Metadata API calls under the hood. Not every type has identical full support — Salesforce's Metadata Coverage Report documents real differences, so the second option is also false.

questions.prompt: Which command moves metadata FROM an org INTO your local project?
options: sf project deploy start
sf project retrieve start
sf org create scratch
sf package install
questions.explain: sf project retrieve start pulls metadata from an org into local source-format files; sf project deploy start moves in the opposite direction, local project into the org.

questions.prompt: A deploy to a production org includes Apex classes and triggers, and no --test-level flag was passed. Which test level applies, and why can't NoTestRun be used here?
options: RunLocalTests applies by default; NoTestRun is restricted to development-type orgs (sandbox, Developer Edition, trial, scratch) and is never allowed for production
NoTestRun always applies by default regardless of target org type
RunAllTestsInOrg applies by default, including every installed package's tests
The deploy fails immediately with no test level specified
questions.explain: RunLocalTests is the default production behavior when Apex is involved, running every test in the org except those from installed managed/unlocked packages; NoTestRun is explicitly restricted to development-type targets and can never be used for a production deploy.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce Extension Pack component to what it provides.
right: A dedicated SOQL editor with autocomplete against the org's actual schema
The glue extension letting the rest of the pack call into your installed sf CLI
Component scaffolding and HTML/JS autocomplete tied to the LWC framework's APIs
Syntax highlighting, code completion, and the Apex Replay Debugger
questions.explain: Salesforce CLI Integration connects the pack to your installed CLI; the Apex extension provides language tooling plus the Replay Debugger; the LWC extension provides component scaffolding and framework-aware autocomplete; the SOQL extension provides a schema-aware query editor.

questions.prompt: On a freshly created, source-tracked scratch org, you run sf project deploy start for the very first time, with no narrowing flags. What happens, and why?
options: Nothing deploys, since there's no tracked baseline yet
Every local file deploys, because each one looks "new" relative to an empty tracking baseline
Only files modified in the last 24 hours deploy
The command fails because --source-dir is required on the first run
questions.explain: With no prior sync recorded, source tracking treats every local file as changed relative to the empty baseline, so the first deploy sends the entire project; only later deploys are limited to what actually changed since the last sync.

questions.prompt: A company wants to share a set of custom objects and Apex utilities across its own several internal orgs, with no need to hide the implementation. Which package type best fits?
options: A second-generation managed package
An unlocked package
A first-generation managed package
No packaging is possible for this use case
questions.explain: Unlocked packages are developer-controlled, with visible (often editable) metadata — a strong fit for internal, cross-org application metadata where hiding implementation from your own teams would be counterproductive.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about promoting a second-generation managed package version to released.
options: The Dev Hub user must hold the "Promote a Package Version to Released" permission
The package version must meet Apex code coverage requirements
A given package version number can be promoted and released exactly once, and it cannot be undone
Promotion automatically reverts the version back to beta after 90 days
Beta versions can be listed for general distribution on AppExchange without promotion
questions.explain: Promotion requires the specific Dev Hub permission and adequate code coverage, and is a one-way, one-time action per version number. Promoted versions do not revert automatically, and beta versions specifically cannot be generally distributed on AppExchange until promoted.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in a package version number formatted MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.BUILD, the ________ segment is assigned automatically by the Dev Hub, often written as the literal value NEXT.
questions.explain: The Dev Hub automatically increments the BUILD segment every time a new version is created at the same MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; writing "1.2.0.NEXT" tells the Dev Hub to compute it.

questions.prompt: What does Salesforce recommend regarding how many namespaces an organization should use across its 2GP managed packages?
options: A brand-new namespace for every single package
A single namespace shared across all of an organization's 2GP managed packages, since it makes cross-package code sharing easier
No namespace should ever be registered for managed packages
A new namespace for every package version
questions.explain: Salesforce explicitly recommends sharing a single namespace across all of an organization's 2GP managed packages, since it simplifies code sharing between packages in the same namespace.

questions.prompt: Match each packaging/org-setup concept to its correct description.
right: A registered prefix applied to a managed package's components to prevent naming collisions
A captured copy of an org's features, settings, licenses, and limits, without data or metadata content
An immutable, installable snapshot of a package's contents at a point in time
A captured copy of a scratch org's metadata and data together, as a reusable starting point
questions.explain: An org shape captures configuration only (no data/metadata); an org snapshot captures metadata and data together; a namespace is a collision-preventing prefix; a package version is an immutable, installable snapshot of a package's actual contents.

questions.prompt: Which restriction applies to a scratch org being used as the source for creating a new org snapshot?
options: It must be at least 30 days old
It can't itself have been created from a snapshot, and it can't have been created with a namespace
It must have zero custom objects deployed
It must be the Dev Hub's own default org
questions.explain: A scratch org can only serve as a snapshot source if it wasn't itself created from a snapshot and wasn't created with a namespace.

questions.prompt: What does the --plan flag add when running sf data export tree across a query that spans multiple related objects?
options: It increases the per-query record limit beyond 2,000
It generates one JSON file per object plus a plan definition file preserving the parent-child relationships for re-import
It converts the exported data into CSV format
It automatically imports the data into a second org immediately
questions.explain: --plan produces separate JSON data files per object involved, plus a plan definition file (ending -plan.json) tying them together so relationships are preserved when the data is later imported.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about package versioning and ancestry.
options: versionName is a free-text label with no effect on install logic or version ordering
An ancestor version declares the specific prior version a new version is meant to upgrade from
The MAJOR, MINOR, and PATCH segments are all assigned automatically by the Dev Hub
sf package version list shows all versions across a developer's packages
Ancestry only matters for unlocked packages, never managed packages
questions.explain: versionName is a human label with no functional effect; ancestry declares the specific upgrade-from version; sf package version list lists all versions. MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH are developer-set, not Dev Hub-assigned (only BUILD is automatic), and ancestry is specifically called out as a managed-package concern in this course, not an unlocked-package one.

questions.prompt: Put these practice-lab steps in the correct order for a full create-deploy-sync-dispose round trip.
items: Create the scratch org with sf org create scratch
Deploy the project's source with sf project deploy start
Make a change locally or directly in the org
Sync that change in the needed direction (deploy or retrieve)
Delete the scratch org with sf org delete scratch
questions.explain: The round trip runs: create the org, deploy the current project into it, make a change on either side, sync that specific change in the right direction, and finally delete the scratch org deliberately rather than letting it expire.

questions.prompt: A developer runs sf org create scratch and gets a "no default Dev Hub found" error. Which command should they run first to diagnose which of the three possible causes applies?
options: sf project deploy preview
sf org list
sf data export tree
sf package version create list
questions.explain: sf org list immediately shows whether any org is authenticated and flagged as a Dev Hub, and whether one is marked default — distinguishing between "never enabled," "never authenticated," and "authenticated but not default."

questions.prompt: A file isn't being deployed and the developer suspects a .forceignore pattern is unintentionally excluding it. What's the recommended first step to confirm this, rather than assuming the deploy command is broken?
options: Delete .forceignore entirely and redeploy
Run sf project deploy preview, which explicitly lists anything being ignored
Re-create the scratch org from scratch
Switch to a different sourceApiVersion
questions.explain: sf project deploy preview explicitly surfaces what a deploy would ignore due to .forceignore rules, immediately confirming whether a forceignore pattern — not a deploy bug — is the real cause.

questions.prompt: Select every true best practice described in this course's final lesson.
options: Commit sfdx-project.json, config/, .forceignore, and force-app/ to version control
Delete scratch orgs deliberately once you're done with them, rather than letting them passively expire
Store CLI authentication credentials directly inside a committed project file for convenience
Choose unpackaged, unlocked, or managed packaging deliberately based on actual reuse or distribution needs
Avoid writing Apex tests until just before a production deploy
questions.explain: The best practices are: commit everything required to deploy correctly, dispose of scratch orgs deliberately, and choose a packaging approach based on real reuse/distribution needs. Storing credentials in a committed file and delaying test discipline are both explicitly called out as things NOT to do.

questions.prompt: Scratch org creation fails because the Dev Hub has hit its active scratch org allocation limit. What's the actual fix?
options: Pass a --force flag to override the limit
Delete scratch orgs you're done with, rather than letting unused ones accumulate until they expire naturally
Switch the Dev Hub to a different sourceApiVersion
Re-register the Dev Hub's namespace
questions.explain: There's no override flag for this — the real fix is actively deleting scratch orgs you've finished with instead of letting a growing pile of unused ones sit around counting against the Dev Hub's active allocation.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when a deploy or retrieve reports a conflict (the same component changed both locally and in the org since the last sync), the flag that forces the operation to proceed anyway is ________.
questions.explain: --ignore-conflicts forces a deploy or retrieve through despite detected conflicts, keeping whichever side is being actively pushed or pulled — a deliberate choice since it can overwrite the other side's change.
